labels.name: P4
labels.description: Work the maintainer asked for, for the next cut

body:
**The request (mkinney, 2026-11-15):** "Do we need to handle svg file import?" ... "Yes file it". Many waterjet, laser and plasma users draw in Inkscape or Illustrator and export SVG. WAZER's own app takes SVG and DXF (see #1525).

## What

Import an SVG file as 2D sketch geometry for 2D operations (Contour, Pocket, Engrave/Trace, plasma or waterjet profile). It goes into the same sketch entity as the DXF import, so the operations need no new input path.

## Depends on

- #1860 (DXF core reader), #1861 (2D sketch chaining, outer-vs-hole nesting, open chains) and #1862 (the sketch ECS entity, .camproj persistence, undoable import).
- Stack on those: the SVG reader only produces sketch chains and reuses chaining, nesting and the import command.

## Scope

- **Elements:** `path` (M/L/H/V/C/S/Q/T/A/Z, absolute and relative), `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `rect` (with rx/ry), `circle`, `ellipse`. `g` groups with `transform` (matrix, translate, scale, rotate, skew), applied to the geometry.
- **Curves:** cubic and quadratic Béziers and elliptical arcs become arcs or polylines within the document's chord tolerance. An arc stays an arc where it is circular after the transform.
- **Units and scale:** `width`/`height` with units (mm, cm, in, pt, pc, px), and the `viewBox`. px uses 96 px/in (the CSS rule). If the file states no physical size, the import asks for the scale. It never guesses silently.
- **Y axis:** SVG Y points down. Flip it so the drawing appears as it does in the editor.
- **Ignored, with a note:** fill, stroke style, text (unless converted to paths), images, clip paths, masks, `use` references to symbols outside the file.
- **Refusals, by name:** a malformed path, a zero or negative size, a degenerate arc, and a file larger than the import budget give a clear error, never a panic (the Prime Directive).
- **MCP:** an `import_svg` tool, or the shared sketch-import tool with format svg (AGENTS.md "Commands ship with an MCP tool").

## Not in scope (later)

- Text to outlines (fonts), embedded images, and CSS stylesheets.

## Done means

- A fixture SVG set (a rectangle with a hole, Bézier and arc shapes, a nested group with transforms, mm and in documents, and one file without a physical size) imports to the expected sketch chains. The tests pin the chain count, closure, nesting and size within tolerance.
- A 2D Contour on an imported SVG posts. A golden is pinned for one plasma or waterjet-style profile.
- Malformed fixtures are refused by name and never panic. The importer fuzz test covers the SVG reader.
- The user guide import page (and #1525's waterjet notes) lists SVG.

Related: #1525 (waterjet research), #1452 (DXF umbrella), #1860-#1870 (DXF chain).

title: Fanuc lathe G76: four schedule readings are unverified; a wrong Z-shift or end-Z reading moves a flank thread axially or into a shoulder

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: blocked
labels.description: Waiting on another issue or a decision

labels.name: area:turning
labels.description: Lathe and mill-turn

labels.name: area:post
labels.description: Post processors and G-code

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
## What is open

The Fanuc lathe post (`assets/posts/fanuc-lathe.cps`) can write the two-block G76 thread cycle (post option G76 cycle). The post models the control's pass schedule from public Fanuc-compatible references (GSK988TA manual, LinuxCNC G76 for the flank sign). No source that we read states four readings of that schedule. No run on a Fanuc control or on a Fanuc simulator confirms them. The PathPilot Hub simulation cannot check them, because its lathe uses the LinuxCNC one-block `G76 P.. J.. K..`.

Found in the full review of PR #517 (https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/517#pullrequestreview-5910390160). The readings are recorded in `docs/decisions/417-g76-matches-verified.md`.

In the table, k is the thread height and a is the tool angle of the first block (twice the flank angle).

| Item | Reading that the post uses | What a wrong reading can do | Threads affected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Z-shift sign, and which pass sits at the programmed Z | Deeper passes move in the direction of travel (LinuxCNC sign). The post sets the start Z to `c_first - k*tan(a/2)`, so pass n starts at `start + depth_n*tan(a/2)`. | The whole thread moves axially by `k*tan(a/2)` to `2k*tan(a/2)`. For the golden `thread_g76_area.nc` (2 mm lead) that is 0.6 to 1.25 mm. This is a cut in the wrong place. | Flank threads only (a not 0) |
| 2. End-Z shift | Each pass ends at the programmed end Z. | If the control also shifts the end of each pass by `depth*tan(a/2)`, the root pass ends `k*tan(a/2)` past the end Z. At a shoulder, the tool can cut into the shoulder. | Flank threads only (a not 0) |
| 3. Minimum-depth clamp | Q(dmin) is a per-pass minimum against the previous clamped depth. | The pass count or the per-pass depth changes. The root does not change. The control can cut fewer, deeper passes than the verdict judged (the tool load is not judged). | Constant-area ladders. Equal-depth ladders (the default) are not affected. |
| 4. Rounding | Words are whole least increments. R comes from the rounded ladder and is refused beyond one increment. | The pass count is fixed. Single rungs of a long sqrt ladder can differ from the laid ones by a few increments. This is not a gouge. | Long sqrt ladders |

The default radial thread (a = 0) has no Z shift. Items 1 and 2 do not change it. Main already writes the flank angle and the flank start (#416). Thus this risk is on main now. PR #517 does not add it.

## Priority

`P3`. A wrong reading of item 1 or 2 is wrong posted G-code (a `P1` class). But no source shows that the reading is wrong, and the defect is not shown. A workaround exists: the default output is the G32 chain, which does not use the control's schedule, and the default infeed is radial. If a control run shows that item 1 or 2 is wrong, raise this issue to `P1`.

## Open question (do not implement here)

Must the Fanuc post refuse, or warn, for a flank-angle G76 (a not 0) until items 1 and 2 are verified? A refusal makes the output safe now, but it removes a cycle that can be correct. A warning keeps the cycle but can be ignored. Decide this before the control run, or with its result.

## Done means

- A run on a Fanuc lathe control, or on the vendor's simulator, posts the goldens `thread_g76.nc` (mm and inch) and `thread_g76_area.nc`.
- The run records, for each pass: the start Z, the end Z and the depth.
- Each of the four items is confirmed, or the post is changed to the control's reading with a pinning test.
- `docs/decisions/417-g76-matches-verified.md` (or a new decision entry) records the result.
- The open question above has a recorded answer.

title: M12.1: solidcore's tight bounding box takes the whole cylinder of a trimmed face (Milling-test.step: Y max 30.0, true 19.719), plus two smaller findings at pin 55d0e763

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: blocked
labels.description: Waiting on another issue or a decision

labels.name: area:3d
labels.description: 3D milling and finishing

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
Found by the STEP bench of #916 (`crates/kernel/tests/step_agreement.rs`), at the solidcore pin `55d0e7638b9e1ebbf91ab8c10657e595c114ecda`.

**1. Wrong bounding box (the one that matters).**
`testdata/models/Milling-test.step` (and its inch twin) is a 60 mm disc with a flat at Y = 19.719. Imported through `camcraft_kernel::solidcore_step`, the solid's volume (52808.744 mm^3) and area (11143.378 mm^2) agree with truck's mesh to 1.2e-4, but `StepSolid::measure`'s box - the port's `calculate_bounding_box` with `tight: true` - is `[-30, -30, -5]..[30, 30, 20]`. The file's own vertices, truck's mesh and solidcore's own mesh (`solidcore-tess`) all stop at Y = 19.719. The box takes the whole R = 30 cylinder, not the trimmed face. It is pinned in the bench as `disagree: bounding box`.

Not known yet: whether the port's box is wrong for any trimmed periodic face, or whether the record-to-kernel build (`solidcore_convert::brep::to_kernel_body`) gives the face a parameter box that covers the whole circle. A kernel-made fixture (a cylinder cut by a plane through the seam's own booleans) would tell the two apart.

Why P1: stage 5 (#917) puts imported geometry under every toolpath. A box 10 mm too large would mis-size automatic stock and mis-place anything aligned to the part's extent.

**2. Stale cached topology after the build.** `to_kernel_body` hands out a B-rep whose cached `Face::shell` is behind its face-use links on every fixture; the port's `topology::integrity::check` refuses it ("cached face shell: face 0 not found"). The seam works around it with `Brep::refresh_cached_topology()` (public; rewrites the cached fields only). To report upstream (tangency-labs/solidcore); the maintainer decides who files it there.

**3. No cancellation in the STEP topology pass.** `solidcore_step::topology::read_solids` takes no progress or cancel hook, so the importer's time bound cannot stop it; it is bounded only by the reader's caps and the seam's 64 MiB size bound. To raise upstream, or to bound by calling the per-solid readers from the seam.

Part of #27. Gates #917.

Done means: the Milling-test rows of the bench read `agree` (the box fixed at its source, or the importer taking its box from a source that is right, with the reason recorded), the root cause is named in a decision entry, and findings 2 and 3 are either fixed at a new pin or filed upstream with their links here.

PR #913 (`Refs #900`) makes `cargo xtask gate` use sccache as a shared compile cache when it is on PATH, and lightens the dev profile (line-table debug info for our crates, none for dependencies, dependency `opt-level` 1). What to do, on the PR's branch (`issue/900-build-cache`) or on `main` once #913 is merged:
1. Without sccache installed: `cargo xtask gate quick --dry-run` and one real `cargo xtask gate test <any test name>` - the gate must run exactly as before (no wrapper set, no error).

Install sccache, then build the same test binary from an empty `target/` twice in two different checkouts or worktrees: note the cold time, the second (warm cache) time, the `sccache --show-stats` hit rate and the `target/` size. 4. Check a panic backtrace of a failing test still shows file:line with the new debug settings.
5. Is the C code (flecs, built through `cc`) cached on Linux? On Windows/MSVC it is not.

Report the numbers and anything that broke as a comment here (and on #913 if it is still open). A fix, if one is needed, is a small PR against `xtask/` (a process file: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`).

body:
Found while working #864 (a STEP model imported coarser than the importer promises is flagged, its gouge verdicts tightened, and refused past that).

**What #864's PR does.** A reduced-fidelity model carries its achieved error. The gouge laws of the upright mill kinds subtract the excess from their tolerance while a positive tolerance is left: the section law (b), the solid law (b2), the envelope law's gouge half (f), `generate::contain_into`, the lathe's axial hole verdict, and the program sim's deviation tolerance. Past that, the program gate refuses by name.

**What is owed.** Everything below is safe today (refused, or stricter than before), but less useful than it should be.

1. **Kinds refused outright on any reduced-fidelity model**, because their gouge laws do not read the excess yet (`operation::fidelity_law::excess_aware`):
   - the cone and engrave rides: 2D chamfer, deburr, trace, engrave (generator construction laws);
   - probe, and the cross drill (`operation/cross_part.rs`, `SolidLaw { allow: GOUGE_TOL }`);
   - the multi-axis kinds (`motion` `multiaxis/entry_ramp.rs`, `stamp*.rs`, `rotary_links.rs`) and the rotary kinds (`operation/rotary_law.rs`, `allow` and `rapid_allow`);
   - turning (`motion` `turning/revolve.rs`, `form.rs`, `thread.rs`; `blade_warnings`, `thread_warnings`, `form_warnings`);
   - plasma.
   Each needs `material.excess` threaded into its law and the kind added to `excess_aware`. A metre-unit STEP file is always reduced fidelity (next point), so these kinds cannot post on one today.
2. **Collision laws are not tightened**: shank and holder reach (`sim` `verify/reach.rs`), rapids in stock (`verify/rapids.rs`, `rapids_posed.rs`, `rapids_radial.rs`), the turning rapid, bar-feed and holder scans (`margin: GOUGE_TOL` in `generate.rs`). They judge clearance against rest material. While an operation still posts the excess is under 0.01 mm, so a clearance can read up to that much too generous on a convex wall.
3. **A metre-unit STEP file** stops at the kernel's least tolerance (1e-5 m = 0.01 mm, #839) and is flagged reduced fidelity with half the verdict tolerance left. Scaling the geometry to millimetres before meshing would remove the cause.
4. **The facet budget is not a user setting.** The refusal says "re-import with a larger budget" (the maintainer's wording on #864), but `MAX_FACETS` is a constant. The import dialog, the script verb and MCP `import_model` need a budget the user can raise.
5. **Display tolerances** still read the plain 0.01 mm on a reduced-fidelity model: the machined-surface classes (`machined_classes.rs`) and the viewport preview (`ui` `trace/eye.rs`, `cpu_eye.rs`). The binding verdict is tightened; the colours are not.
6. **The envelope law (f) and the containment solid law** are tightened through the same helper as (b) but have no fixture-level pin of their own on a reduced-fidelity model.

Done means: each kind in (1) is either judged with tightened laws or stays refused for a stated reason; the laws in (2) grow their bands by the excess; (3) and (4) are decided and built or closed with the reason; pins for (6).

title: Build cycle: every worktree compiles the whole dependency tree cold - share a compile cache, cut debug info, use a faster linker

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
Raised by the maintainer (2026-11-11): "why are we cold building complete bundles .. the tests are localized to crates".

## What happens today (measured on the dev machine)
- Every issue worker, reviewer and gate works in its own worktree with its own `target/`. A fresh one compiles the WHOLE dependency tree before the first test runs: about 15-25 minutes per review and 25-75 minutes per gate, almost all of it third-party crates (flecs' C through bindgen/cc, wgpu/egui, the B-rep kernel, the script engine ...), not our code.
- `Cargo.toml` sets `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2`: every dependency is optimised in dev builds. That makes tests run faster but makes each cold build much slower.
- Nothing sets `debug`, so dev builds carry full debug info for all crates: one `target/` reaches 50-120 GB (the disk filled twice today) and every link is slow.
- Integration tests are one binary per file: `crates/app/tests` has 266 files, motion 65, sim 50. The batch gate's app step takes about 24 of its 38 minutes, much of it linking and starting 266 binaries.
- `.cargo/config.toml` holds only the `xtask` alias: no linker choice, no cache wrapper. `sccache` is not installed; `rust-lld` is.

## Wanted (this issue: the three cheap ones, measured)
1. **A shared compile cache across worktrees** (`sccache` as `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and as the C compiler wrapper for the cc-built C code if that works on MSVC). Registry crates live at the same path for every worktree, so their compilations are cache hits; a fresh worktree should then compile only our own crates. It must be OPTIONAL: a machine without sccache builds exactly as today (enable it from `cargo xtask` / the gate wrappers when `sccache` is on PATH, or document the env var - never hard-code a wrapper in `.cargo/config.toml` that breaks a machine without it). Say how to install it and how big its cache is allowed to grow.
2. **Less debug info**: `debug = false` (or `"line-tables-only"`) for dependencies, and line tables only for our crates in dev/test - enough for backtraces and panics with file:line. Report target size and link time before/after.
3. **A faster linker** for the Windows MSVC target (`rust-lld` / `lld-link`), and the equivalent on Linux/macOS where it helps, again without breaking a machine that lacks it.
4. Re-examine `opt-level = 2` for all dependencies: keep it only for the crates whose speed the tests need (measure: batch gate time with opt-level 2 everywhere vs 1 vs a short list).

Measure and report, on the same machine, cold (empty target, warm cache where a cache applies) and warm: `cargo test -p camcraft-app --no-run`, `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test <one binary>`, `cargo xtask gate quick` on a one-file app change, and the `target/` size. No test may change behaviour; the gates stay green.

## Not in this issue (file separately if the numbers say so)
- Folding the 266 one-file app test binaries into a few binaries (one per area, files as modules). This is the biggest structural win for the gate, but it changes the gate maps in `xtask` and every "run this binary" instruction.

## Process
`.cargo/config.toml`, `xtask/` and the gate wrappers are process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, and say in the PR what a fork must do.

Done means: a fresh worktree reaches its first app test at least 3x faster than today with the cache warm, `target/` is at most half today's size, the settings are optional per machine and documented, and the measured numbers are in the PR.

body:
The chamfer/taper kind is a sharp cone only: no tip diameter, no tip radius, and no tapered flank above a non-sharp tip.

**Where:** `Taper` is "a cone widening upward from its virtual sharp tip" (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs`, Taper doc; `is_sane` near `:305`).

**Effect:**
- Flat-tip chamfer mills, V-engravers with a point radius, countersinks and combined center drills (both with a real tip diameter), and tapered end mills with a ball or flat tip can't be described.
- Writing them as sharp cones misstates where the cutter actually is: the depth for a given chamfer width is wrong by the tip.

**Fix sketch:** `Taper` gains an optional tip diameter and tip radius (and a tip form: flat or ball). The chamfer-depth math, the sim and the gouge laws use the real tip.

Effort: max (geometry).

**Done means:** a flat-tip chamfer and a radiused-point V-bit chamfer to the right width at the right depth; pinned.

body:
There's no thread-mill tool kind.

**Where:** `ToolKind` (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs:23`) has `Tap` and the lathe `Thread` insert, but no single-form or multi-form thread mill.

**Effect:** thread milling is a common job on small CNC mills (interpolated threads in any material, large or odd sizes, no tap breakage). A vendor tool library can't carry thread mills at all. In one real catalog build, over 300 thread mills had to be left out.

**Fix sketch:**
- New kinds: single-form (one tooth, any pitch within range) and multi-form (several teeth, a fixed pitch). Each carries cutter diameter, form angle, pitch or pitch range, teeth count, neck and shank.
- A thread-milling operation: helical interpolation, internal and external, climb or conventional, single or multi pass, radial passes.
- Simulation and gouge laws for the form.

Effort: max (a new kind, a helical op and the sim).

**Done means:** a thread mill can be stored and used by a thread-milling op that verifies clean and posts helical G2/G3 with Z; pinned with goldens.

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

labels.name: enhancement

labels.name: P8

body:
Found while working #586 (M7.3 3/6). Part of #26.

**Why #586 can't finish as a seam move:** every app stock *holder* is either a plain grid or the **carried `Body`** (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/carry.rs`). `Body` stores the stock carried between setups as **two-sided columns**: `pub dex: Dexel` plus a per-column floor (`on_floor` / `on_mesh`). It supports the setup-change transforms that `LatticeTurn` makes exact on a lattice: XY quarter turns, Z flips and mirrors (`carry`, `deviate`'s Z-mirror via `Dexel::from_grid`, `display()`).

The app also **mutates** it as a column store:
- `simulate(&mut body.dex, ..)` in `rest/across.rs` and `rest.rs`;
- `stock_sim_carry`'s clip loop writing `dex.lower(..)`;
- `Held::Plain(Dexel)` / `Held::Carried(Body)` and `dex_mut()`.

Swapping `Dexel` for `Stock` there is a **data-model change**: carried stock on the field engine.

**Open design questions:**
1. **Representation:** the field engine holds a solid as a narrow-band SDF plus cut layers. Carrying it is a rigid transform of the field (a re-sample, or a transformed query frame) rather than a lattice permutation. Is a transformed query frame (no re-sample) exact enough for the verdicts?
2. **Floors:** a flipped part's floor is the former top. The field is a closed solid, so it has no separate floor, but "a column cut through" needs an equivalent read.
3. **Clipping** to a later setup's own stock: a field intersection (max of SDFs) replaces `lower`.
4. **Equivalence:** a heavy-lane agreement test of the carried verdicts (`setup_carry`, `rest_across_setups`, `carried_verify`) on both engines, like `stock_engine_agreement`.

**Done means:** `stock_sim_carry`, `rest`, `rest/across` and the operation priors hold carried stock as `Stock`. A field-engine carry passes the same carried-stock suites, plus an agreement lane against the column carry. #586 can then close. This is a prerequisite of #589.

Related: #26, #585 (PR #595), #586, #589, #633 (PR #636, the field block speed fix this depends on).

title: Trochoidal toolpaths: constant-engagement loops for slots, channels and corners (Adaptive mode + standalone op)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: area:3d
labels.description: 3D milling and finishing

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.name: P8
labels.description: Larger idea needing design or research before code

body:
## What

A **trochoidal toolpath strategy**: circular loops whose centre advances along the cut. It's the usual constant-engagement way to clear slots, narrow channels and corners, where a spiral or offset adaptive path would be forced into full-width (or a sudden jump in) radial engagement. Ship it as a selectable option for Adaptive clearing (2D and 3D levels), and as a standalone "Trochoidal slot" operation along a chain or centre line.

This is a feature request. The existing trochoid work (#5, #47, the M11.4 fallbacks) only covers Adaptive's *internal* fallback in slot-width channels and thin bands. This issue is the general, user-facing strategy.

## Background (public literature)

- **Geometry**, for a simple circular loop: x(φ) = B·cos φ, y(φ) = B·sin φ + S·φ/(2π), with B the loop radius and S the forward advance per revolution. For a slot of width W cut by a tool of diameter D, B = (W − D)/2. Epicycloidal and double-trochoid variants also exist.
- **Engagement angle** θ = θ_out − θ_in: the centre angle of the cutter's contact arc with the *current* stock, read at each point along the path.
- **Chip thickness** in the peripheral approximation is h(α) = f_z·sin α. On a trochoid the engagement window moves along the loop, so h varies; it isn't constant.
- **How constant engagement is kept:** evaluate θ against the live stock, and when it exceeds the limit, shrink the loop, cut the forward step, or reshape the loop, and/or drop the feed where θ rises.
- **References:**
  - Otkur & Lazoglu, "Trochoidal milling", IJMTM 2007: chip-thickness and force model, double trochoid.
  - Rauch, Duc & Hascoet, "Improving trochoidal tool paths generation and implementation using process constraints modelling", IJMTM 2009.
  - B-spline trochoid optimisation with a maximum-engagement constraint, Int J Adv Manuf Technol 2022 (doi 10.1007/s00170-022-09527-z).
  - Circular, trochoidal and epicycloidal parameterisations, Prod. Eng. 2021 (doi 10.1007/s11740-021-01060-4).

## Proposed parameters (user parameters with defaults)

- loop width (≤ the channel width − D, auto from the channel when unset)
- forward step per loop
- maximum engagement angle (or the equivalent optimal load)
- return arc: cutting / non-cutting with microlift (height) / retract
- feed on the cutting arc vs the return arc (the return arc at a higher "air" feed)
- direction: climb / conventional
- smoothing radius for the loop-to-loop transitions

## Done means

1. A trochoid generator in `crates/motion` that is engagement-controlled against the in-process stock: the loop and step adapt so θ ≤ the limit everywhere, and a refusal by name where the channel is narrower than the tool or the limit can't be met.
2. Adaptive gets a "trochoidal in slots/corners" mode that switches from the spiral to trochoidal loops where the spiral would exceed the limit (merges with, or replaces, #5's internal fallback).
3. A standalone Trochoidal slot operation along a picked chain or centre line, through `CreateOperation` / `EditOperationParams` with undo.
4. The verifier judges the loops: no gouge, the engagement limit holds (a measured θ trace in tests), and microlift returns land on air (#47).
5. Pins:
   - a full-width slot with θ_max under the limit, compared with a straight slot at 180°;
   - a corner that a spiral path overloads, cut within the limit;
   - a too-narrow channel refused by name;
   - post goldens on Fanuc, where arcs are written as G2/G3 when the post supports them.

Related: #5, #7, #44, #47 (Adaptive trochoid internals).

body:
Follow-up from #5 round 2 (staged on worktree agent-af493aee8d4f2d538, gated off).

The trochoid fallback (spiral -> trochoid -> rings) is wired in `pocket_hsm` / `pocket_troch` and plans the 22x60 channel end to end. One law keeps it off:

1. **Landing law (one descent per level).** Each microlift return ramps down onto the next front arc's start. That start is already in cut: the crescent ahead and the 0.33 mm wall strip are both inside the measuring rim (r + 1.5 cells). So `quality` counts a descent into stock every loop (118 for 2 levels against the law's 2). The spiral's lifted pieces avoid this with air leads. Trochoid arcs have no air lead that crosses no floor feed: a floor lead from inside the cleared area to the next start crosses the previous arc. Options to try: arcs whose ends sweep the wall strip clean (rho * sin(h) = half-width) plus a start ramp along the arc's own circle extension (crossing-free up to 90 deg + asin(s / 2 rho)), or non-circular loops whose start lies behind the previous envelope. Pinned by `troch_tests::a_landing_on_a_loop_start_in_cut_is_refused_by_name`. Remove the law's refusal once it holds.
2. **A practical step for thin bands (#13's 14 mm band).** It reads rho 1.90, s 0.103 and 2575 loops a level at the load. That is over the `LOOP_CAP` (600) and, before that, has no room to open out behind a helix. A closed band's trochoid is also not wired yet. It stays on the named Offset-rings fallback.
3. The 3-D ladder (`machining3d::hsm`) does not try the trochoid yet (`adaptive_passes(.., false)`).
